title: The everything theory of mass transit - Works in Progress Magazine
gist: US transit agencies have accumulated so many secondary mandates - emissions, equity, union jobs, Buy America content, community input, public art - that each dollar of mission creep is subtracted from frequency and coverage, the only things that actually shift drivers out of cars. The hardest evidence is bus electrification economics: Austin pays $917,000 per electric bus vs $535,000 diesel, Miami-Dade runs about six of 75 electric buses on a given day after Proterra's bankruptcy, and the capital for electrifying a single bus could instead buy roughly 2,300 service hours carrying 30,000+ riders. The article argues congestion pricing and land-use densification dominate electrification on emissions per dollar (66m tons from shorter trips vs 9m tons from mode-switching in 2018).

themes.theme: Mission creep as a cost driver

insights.claim: Public transport agencies are assigned goals - emissions reduction, neighborhood beautification, union job creation, community empowerment - that trade off directly against the core function of moving the maximum number of people.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Cost-per-rider and on-time metrics for US transit are structurally impaired by policy design, not management; underwrite transit capex programs assuming persistent overruns rather than efficiency gains.
insights.quote: All of this impedes public transport’s ability to do its main job: transporting the public.
insights.locator: We ask public transport to address problems

insights.claim: The Boston Green Line extension, finished a decade later than planned, added a three-kilometer bike and pedestrian path costing $20 million after 13 people advocated for it at a community meeting.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A concrete price tag on discretionary scope additions - useful as a benchmark when modeling contingency on US rail extensions.
insights.quote: added a three-kilometer bike and pedestrian path after 13 people advocated for it at a community meeting, at a staggering cost of $20 million
insights.locator: The Transit Costs Project documents

insights.claim: Each layer of government attaches its own mandates to a transit agency's funding: federal domestic-content and prevailing-wage rules (Buy America, CHIPS Act daycare requirements, Davis-Bacon), state environmental review (the California Environmental Quality Act), and local design, public art, local hiring, and engagement requirements.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Multi-source funding is a hidden cost multiplier: projects with federal plus state plus local money should be priced with materially worse unit economics than single-source ones.
insights.locator: The typical transit agency gets funding

insights.claim: Road, highway, and parking construction is held to a much narrower mandate - improving mobility - than transit is, giving car infrastructure a structural cost advantage in public procurement.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Explains why transit keeps losing share to driving on a cost-per-unit-of-mobility basis despite subsidy; a regulatory-symmetry reform would be the real catalyst to watch, not more capital.
insights.locator: Governments build roads, highways, and parking structures

insights.claim: Buses account for less than one percent of US transportation emissions yet operate under more rules and regulations than personal cars do.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Regulatory burden on buses is wildly disproportionate to their emissions footprint - decarbonization capital aimed at bus fleets is chasing under one percent of the problem.
insights.quote: Buses are a rounding error as a proportion of vehicles on the road, accounting for less than one percent of US transportation emissions.
insights.locator: Buses are a rounding error

themes.theme: How transit acquired its extra mandates

insights.claim: Until the mid-twentieth century almost all transit was privately owned with a simple objective function - maximize ridership and fare revenue while minimizing costs - and mission creep began only after governments took over failing lines in the 1960s.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The historical baseline shows the current cost structure is institutional, not technological - relevant to any thesis that privatized or concession-model transit can undercut public agencies.
insights.locator: Transit missions didn't always creep

insights.claim: Because most of the public drove, the political case for continued transit subsidy had to be made to non-users, which pushed agencies to align with the War on Poverty, the Civil Rights Movement, environmentalism, and the oil crisis rather than with rider outcomes.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Identifies the political mechanism producing scope creep - it persists as long as the median funder is a non-rider, so reform will not come from within agencies.
insights.quote: the majority of funding coming from voters who didn’t use it
insights.locator: In the 1960s, governments began taking over

insights.claim: The American Public Transit Association markets transit as a cure-all, claiming it will deliver work, education, healthcare access, job creation, less congestion, and cleaner air simultaneously.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The industry's own advocacy language is the source of the everything-mandate problem - a tell that stated benefit cases in transit funding proposals are systematically overstated.
insights.quote: will get Americans to work, to education, and to healthcare, and it will also get our nation to more job creation, less traffic congestion and cleaner air
insights.locator: Today, the American Public Transit Association touts

insights.claim: Austin's CapMetro pays $917,000 for a 40-foot electric bus versus $535,000 for the diesel equivalent, a roughly 71 percent procurement premium before operating costs.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Hard capex spread for anyone modeling electric bus OEM demand or municipal fleet budgets - the premium is far above typical EV price-parity assumptions.
insights.locator: Austin's CapMetro 40-foot electric buses

insights.claim: Miami-Dade's transit agency spent roughly $1.1 million per electric bus and, out of 75 purchased, only about six are operating on a given day because they break down every 600 miles - seven times as often as diesel buses.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: An eight percent availability rate on an $82m fleet purchase is the strongest single argument against near-term electric bus procurement; expect procurement pullback and warranty/reliability litigation risk.
insights.quote: out of the 75 buses it purchased, only about six are operating
insights.locator: In south Florida, the Miami-Dade county's transit agency

insights.claim: Proterra's bankruptcy has made replacement parts for already-purchased electric buses difficult to obtain, compounding the fleet's downtime.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Supplier-solvency risk is a first-order variable in transit electrification, not a footnote - buyers should price OEM balance sheets, and it is a cautionary precedent for other thinly capitalized EV manufacturers.
insights.locator: particularly since the manufacturer, Proterra, filed for bankruptcy

insights.claim: Buy American rules mean US agencies pay nearly twice the roughly $600,000 that a standard 12-meter electric bus sells for in Europe, where Chinese manufacturers compete freely.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A quantified protectionism tax of roughly 2x on a decarbonization input - a template for how domestic-content rules erode the volume of green infrastructure actually delivered per dollar.
insights.locator: In Europe, where Chinese manufacturers compete freely

insights.claim: The US electric bus market remains small - about 7,000 electric out of roughly 63,000 buses, and 5,000 of those 7,000 are school buses - leaving transit agencies with few competing suppliers.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Only about 2,000 non-school electric transit buses exist in the US: the addressable market is far thinner than headline electrification targets imply, and thin markets sustain the price premium.
insights.locator: Out of roughly 63,000 buses in the US

insights.claim: Germany's bus fleet electrification raised operating costs by 12 percent, and Stockholm research puts the operator cost increase at at least 16 percent depending on the charging setup, even though passengers experience no difference.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A 12-16 percent structural opex increase with zero rider-facing benefit means electrification is a pure subsidy sink absent a carbon price that clears that bar.
insights.locator: In Germany, electrifying bus fleets increased costs

insights.claim: Converting a diesel bus fleet to electric requires new software, land use permitting, grid connections for charging infrastructure, and additional worker time to fuel vehicles, with route planning around chargers adding significant operational complexity.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The ancillary spend - depot electrification, permitting, dispatch software - is where the real dollars sit, pointing to grid-interconnect and fleet-software vendors rather than bus OEMs as the exposure.
insights.locator: Moving from diesel to electric buses doesn't just mean swapping vehicles

insights.claim: At a median US bus operating cost of $131 per hour and a median 14.3 passengers carried per hour, the money used to electrify a single bus could instead fund roughly 2,300 additional service hours carrying at least 30,000 additional riders.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A ready-made unit-economics test for any transit capital decision: convert capex into forgone service hours and riders before approving it.
insights.locator: Assuming the median cost per hour for operating a bus

insights.claim: Every dollar spent complying with Buy America or staging community meetings is a dollar not spent on improving service frequency or coverage.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Frames compliance spending as directly cannibalizing the service quality that drives ridership and farebox revenue - the key variable for transit credit and ridership forecasts.
insights.quote: Every dollar spent complying with Buy America or staging community meetings is a dollar not spent improving frequency or coverage.
insights.locator: Every dollar spent complying with Buy America

insights.claim: Six California transportation pilot programs - electric carshare, bikeshare, and microtransit in disadvantaged areas funded by the California Air Resources Board - improved mobility for households mostly earning under $25,000 a year but added 128,880 net new vehicle miles and slightly increased overall emissions.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Green mobility pilots can be net emissions-additive while succeeding on equity - a direct warning that dual-mandate programs should not be underwritten on their climate claims.
insights.quote: the programs added 128,880 net new vehicle miles and slightly increased overall emissions rather than decreasing them
insights.locator: The transit tradeoff

insights.claim: Research on Stockholm's busiest bus route found that better pricing of roads and transit plus running buses more often delivered more benefit than electrifying the buses.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Ranks demand-side pricing above supply-side electrification on cost-effectiveness - the policy path that would actually move mode share, and the one with fiscal upside rather than drain.
insights.locator: Prices make perfect

insights.claim: London's congestion charge cut vehicle greenhouse gas emissions by 16 percent, generated £227 million in a single year, and coincided with nine percent fewer traffic accidents in its first year.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Congestion charging is revenue-positive and emissions-negative simultaneously - a fiscally attractive template for cities facing transit funding gaps, and a watch item for municipal budget forecasts.
insights.locator: In London, greenhouse gas emissions from vehicles fell

insights.claim: Switching people from driving to transit saved nine million metric tons of carbon in 2018, but shortening travel distances through more efficient land use could prevent 66 million metric tons - roughly seven times as much.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Land use, not vehicle technology, is the dominant decarbonization lever in transportation - a reason to weight zoning and density reform above fleet electrification in climate-policy exposure.
insights.locator: Switching people from driving to transit saved nine million

insights.claim: Increasing transit service frequency by one percent boosts ridership by about 0.5 percent, and once buses arrive every ten minutes the service becomes appealing to riders who have alternatives, creating a self-reinforcing loop of revenue and quality.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A quantified frequency elasticity of 0.5 plus a ten-minute headway threshold gives a concrete operating target to judge whether an agency's spending will actually grow ridership.
insights.quote: Once buses arrive every ten minutes, bus services become more appealing for riders with alternatives.
insights.locator: When transit becomes more viable and reliable

insights.claim: Electrifying buses makes more sense in major cities where transit is dominant than in car-dominant places such as Fresno, California, where the priority should be moving low-income people to jobs.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Argues for geographically differentiated electrification policy - uniform national fleet mandates misallocate capital in low-density metros.
insights.locator: In major cities, where transit is more dominant

themes.theme: Riders, cars, and the equity inversion

insights.claim: While 91.5 percent of American households own at least one car, only 45 percent of transit riders have a vehicle available at home, meaning transit's core constituency is the carless minority.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Quantifies the political-economy trap: transit serves a small captive base while being funded by a driving majority, which sustains scope creep indefinitely.
insights.locator: While 91.5 percent of American households own

insights.claim: In most of the US, poor people who gain access to a car are more likely to find jobs, keep jobs, find higher-paying jobs, work more hours, get off welfare, and move to better neighborhoods - making car access an anti-poverty intervention.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Directly against the transit-advocacy consensus: mobility outcomes for the poor may be better served by car access programs than by transit capital, a live fault line in transportation policy funding.
insights.quote: Poor people who gain access to a car are more likely to find jobs, keep their jobs, find higher paying jobs, work more hours, get off welfare, and move to better neighborhoods.
insights.locator: Focusing transit on what it does best

insights.claim: Loading environmental and labor mandates onto transit asks people already struggling financially, who already emit far less than most Americans, to carry the cost of decarbonization - which is self-defeating because it makes transit less competitive against cars.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Reframes green transit mandates as regressive: the policy is failing on both its equity and its climate objectives, which is the argument that could eventually reverse funding formulas.
insights.quote: Scope creep fails on its own terms.
insights.locator: Scope creep fails on its own terms

insights.claim: A 2018 UCLA report on Southern California estimated that if one in four rare transit users replaced a single driving trip with transit every two weeks, annual ridership would grow by 96 million.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Shows the ridership upside sits with occasional riders who own cars, not the captive base - so service quality aimed at choice riders is where marginal investment pays.
insights.locator: A 2018 UCLA report on transit ridership

insights.claim: Emissions reduction is better achieved by getting a broad base of people to make small behavioral changes than by forcing a small, already burdened group of transit-dependent riders to carry the load.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The closing policy prescription - broad marginal shifts over concentrated mandates - which favors pricing and land-use instruments over fleet procurement rules.
insights.locator: It's more sensible to reduce emissions
